summary: The Guardian's Jamie Jackson sets out the challenges facing Sir Jim Ratcliffe as he takes charge of Manchester United's sporting side, from Erik ten Hag's uncertain future and John Murtough's position to finding a new CEO. He also covers the crumbling Old Trafford and Carrington facilities, the Glazers' silence with fans, and the tensions of sharing control with the Glazers, who remain majority owners.
one_line: Ratcliffe's in-tray at Manchester United spans Ten Hag's future, football director Murtough, a new CEO, decaying facilities, fan communication and sharing power with the Glazers.
key_facts: Sir Jim Ratcliffe is taking charge of Manchester United's sporting department and may make sweeping changes to posts that directly affect manager Erik ten Hag.
Richard Arnold has left Manchester United despite officially staying until the end of the year; Jean-Claude Blanc, CEO of Ratcliffe's Ineos Sport, may take over the role Ten Hag reports to.

John Murtough, United's football director, has no plans to depart, but some inside the club believe he will be moved sideways or leave; Newcastle's Dan Ashworth and Paul Mitchell (Monaco's sporting director until March) are mentioned as possible replacements.

On a March tour of the club, Ratcliffe questioned the signing of a 30-year-old Casemiro on a four-year deal worth about £350,000 a week; Murtough and Ten Hag, who each hold a transfer veto, were responsible for it.

In the summer Casemiro joined United, Ratcliffe's club Nice made nine signings including Aaron Ramsey and Ross Barkley on frees with one-year deals and Kasper Schmeichel, 35, on a three-year deal in a £1m transfer from Leicester; all three left Nice this summer.

Blanc, 60, holds a Harvard MBA, is billed as the 'Lionel Messi of business' by Nice chief executive Fabrice Bocquet, and has been CEO of Juventus and Paris Saint-Germain, French Tennis, and overseen the Tour de France.
Manchester City have won six championships since United's last in 2013 and have a commercial operation far ahead of United's.

Old Trafford, dating to 1910, has a leaking roof, and Ratcliffe will invest $300m (£237m) into infrastructure, which the article calls small beer compared with the multibillion-pound facelift or new venue needed.
The Carrington training ground has a large footprint but ageing facilities.

No Glazer family member has given a press conference or interview during their 18-year tenure; Ratcliffe, born in Failsworth next to Newton Heath, United's birthplace, is expected to open a regular line to supporters.
Ratcliffe paid an overpriced £1.3bn for his 25% stake; the Glazers remain majority owners, and the 71-year-old oversees football policy.

Ratcliffe admires United's revenue model but is not enamoured of how money is mainly invested in the squad, raising the prospect of conflict if the Glazers block a signing citing a downturn in income.
